title: Do Less With Excellence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues against the common leadership instinct to take on an ever-expanding list of priorities, contending that spreading a team across too many initiatives guarantees mediocrity. The author's core move is to reframe 'doing less' not as a limitation but as a deliberate excellence strategy. Notably, the piece observes that leaders who make this trade-off rarely announce it upward, because senior leaders typically want everything done at once. The piece closes by contrasting how leaders who deliver a few things excellently are perceived as top performers, versus leaders who spread thin, who are seen as merely average and burn out their teams.
points: Teams juggling too many priorities look busy but typically deliver mediocre results.
The best leaders narrow the list of priorities and insist the smaller set be executed with real excellence.
Leaders who choose to focus rarely broadcast that choice upward, since senior leadership usually wants everything delivered simultaneously.
Delivering a few things excellently earns a reputation as a top performer; delivering everything at a mediocre level earns a reputation as merely average, at the cost of burnout.
quotes: When leaders and teams have an ever-expanding list of priorities and initiatives, they generally deliver mediocre results. No one can do many things with excellence.
The best leaders narrow the priorities and demand the team deliver on a small set of initiatives with excellence.
So, informing a more senior leader that you have decided to invest more heavily in some areas over others typically doesn’t go well. Most senior leaders want everything done and then some.
When those same leaders deliver everything asked of them with mediocrity, they are viewed as average performers with team members on the verge of exhaustion and burnout.
Delivering less with excellence is what good leaders do for their teams to prepare them for the marathon of never-ending priorities.
